title: The lending platform, end to end
intro: This is the shape of the systems I own. Pick a component to see what it does, why it exists, what I traded away and what breaks without it — or trace a real journey to see how a decision travels through it.

nodes.label: Lending API
nodes.does: The synchronous surface every lending journey talks to — applications, limit changes, servicing — across Retail and SME credit.
nodes.why: Multiple products need the same loan lifecycle: originate, approve, disburse, service, close. Without one surface, each product reimplements it slightly differently and they drift apart within two releases.
nodes.tradeoff: One shared lifecycle means product-specific behaviour lives behind flags and strategy objects rather than its own service. More indirection to read; the price of not maintaining five divergent copies of the same state machine.
nodes.failure: Product teams build their own flows and the bank ends up with several inconsistent definitions of what 'approved' means.

nodes.label: Underwriting
nodes.does: Assesses applications, with a deduplication stage that catches repeat submissions before they consume assessment capacity.
nodes.why: Duplicate applications waste the most expensive step in the funnel and can produce two different decisions for one applicant.
nodes.tradeoff: The uniqueness guarantee sits in the database as a constraint rather than in application code. That couples correctness to the schema and makes migrations stricter — but application-level checks race under concurrency and a constraint does not.
nodes.failure: Two assessors reach two verdicts on the same person, and whichever writes last wins.

nodes.label: Loan event stream
nodes.does: Kafka topics carrying every state change in a loan's life, partitioned so all events for one account land in order.
nodes.why: Billing, notifications and reconciliation all react to the same state changes. Point-to-point calls would make every new consumer a change to the producer.
nodes.tradeoff: Asynchrony buys decoupling and costs certainty: a consumer can be behind, and 'has it happened yet' stops having an instant answer. Everything downstream must tolerate that.
nodes.failure: Two events for one account process out of order — a reversal applied before its charge produces a balance that is wrong in a way nobody notices until a customer calls.

nodes.label: Billing engine
nodes.does: Turns loan events into monthly statements: interest, fees, VAT, rebates, and automated reconciliation against the ledger.
nodes.why: A statement is the most-read artefact a lending customer receives. An error here is not a data problem, it is a support ticket and a dispute.
nodes.tradeoff: Every handler is idempotent, which costs extra bookkeeping on every write. Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery, so correctness had to come from the consumer being safe to run twice — designing for exactly-once would have been designing against the broker.
nodes.failure: One redelivered event double-charges a customer, and drift is discovered by the customer rather than by us.

nodes.label: Notification service
nodes.does: Consumes lending events and sends repayment reminders and status updates through the delivery providers.
nodes.why: A missed repayment is very often a missed reminder. For repayment behaviour, delivery is not around the product — it is the product.
nodes.tradeoff: Deduplicating before send rather than after means holding recent-send state and accepting a slightly later message. Duplicate reminders erode trust faster than late ones, so latency was the right thing to give up.
nodes.failure: A retry becomes a second message to the customer. Enough of those and people mute the channel — which costs more than the original missed reminder.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.does: System of record for loans, schedules, balances and decisions.
nodes.why: Money needs a single authoritative place where a balance is true, with constraints the application cannot talk its way around.
nodes.tradeoff: Strong consistency over horizontal write scale. For a lending ledger that is not a close call: the volume is manageable and the correctness is not negotiable.
nodes.failure: Nothing downstream can be trusted. Every cache and every statement derives from here.

nodes.label: Read cache
nodes.does: Caches the hot, tolerant reads behind the credit card dashboard.
nodes.why: The dashboard is the screen customers open most, and it was slowest exactly when the most people were looking at it. Tail latency is what a customer experiences as 'the app is slow'.
nodes.tradeoff: Only data that can be slightly stale without misleading anyone is cached. Balances and transaction state are deliberately excluded — a stale balance is worse than a slow one.
nodes.failure: Nothing breaks; it degrades. The cache is an optimisation, and every read still resolves against the system of record on a miss.

nodes.label: Delivery providers
nodes.does: Third-party SMS, email and push channels that actually reach the customer.
nodes.why: Reaching a customer reliably in a specific country is not a problem worth solving in-house.
nodes.tradeoff: An external dependency on the last mile. The consumer treats provider failure as expected rather than exceptional, which is why delivery failure is a tracked number and not an alarm.
nodes.failure: Reminders stop arriving and repayment behaviour degrades before anyone sees an error in our own logs — the argument for measuring delivery, not just sends.

journeys.label: An SME applies for credit
journeys.summary: From submission to a decision the customer can act on.

steps.what: The application arrives with the business's details and requested amount.
steps.decision: Collect the requested amount up front only above a threshold. Asking every applicant for documents they may not need is where SME funnels leak.
Dedupe before assessment, not after. Assessment is the expensive step; spending it twice on one applicant is the waste worth designing out.

steps.what: The decision and its inputs are written as the record of what was decided and why.
steps.decision: Persist the inputs, not just the verdict. A decision you cannot reconstruct is a decision you cannot defend to a regulator.

steps.what: An application-decided event is emitted for anything that needs to react.
steps.decision: Emit the event rather than calling the notifier directly, so adding a consumer later is not a change to underwriting.

steps.what: The applicant is told the outcome.
steps.decision: A declined applicant hears promptly and plainly. Silence after a credit application is the worst outcome for trust, and it is entirely avoidable.

journeys.label: A repayment is about to be missed
journeys.summary: The path that moved on-time repayments by 40%.

steps.what: A repayment-due event is emitted ahead of the date.
steps.decision: Fire ahead of the due date, not on it. A reminder that arrives the morning a payment is due is a notification; one that arrives with time to act is a product.

steps.what: The reminder is composed and deduplicated against recent sends.
steps.decision: Dedupe before sending. Two reminders for one payment reads as a system that does not know what it already told you.

steps.what: The message goes out over SMS, email or push.
steps.decision: Track delivery, not sends. A send that never lands is indistinguishable from success unless you measure the difference.

steps.what: If payment still does not arrive, fees and their VAT are applied on schedule.
steps.decision: Charge only after the reminder path has genuinely been exhausted. A fee for a payment the customer was never told about is a dispute you will lose.

steps.what: A month of loan events is replayed in account-partitioned order.
steps.decision: Order per account, not globally. Global ordering would be simpler to reason about and would not scale past one partition.

steps.what: Interest, fees, VAT and rebates are computed and the statement is assembled.
steps.decision: Every handler is idempotent, so a replay produces the same statement rather than a second set of charges.

steps.what: Automated reconciliation compares the statement against the ledger.
steps.decision: Reconcile automatically every run. Reconciliation that only happens when someone complains is not reconciliation.

steps.what: The statement notification goes to the customer.
steps.decision: Notify only after reconciliation passes. Sending a statement you have not checked turns one bad record into one bad customer conversation.
